In 2006, Apple asked Intel to build the chip for the first iPhone.

Intel said no.

At the time, Intel was worth $116.8 billion.
TSMC, a contract chipmaker in Taiwan, was worth $56.5 billion.

Apple was already putting Intel chips inside Mac computers.
So Steve Jobs went to Intel CEO Paul Otellini first.

Apple set a strict ceiling price and wouldn't budge.
It would pay "not a nickel more" per chip.

Intel's team ran the cost numbers.
The price looked too low, and Intel didn't think the phone would sell in big numbers.

So Intel walked away.

In June 2006, Intel went further.
It sold its mobile chip unit, XScale, to Marvell Technology for $600 million.

Apple turned to ARM architecture instead.
Samsung built the early iPhone chips.

In May 2013, Otellini retired and told The Atlantic what went wrong.
He said "the forecasted cost was wrong and the volume was 100x what anyone thought."

He added: "My gut told me to say yes."

In September 2014, Apple moved its flagship A8 iPhone chip orders to TSMC on its 20nm line.

iPhone volume fueled TSMC's rise in advanced chipmaking.
By November 2020, Apple launched the TSMC-built M1 chip and started dropping Intel from the Mac too.

By July 2025, Apple had sold 3 billion iPhones.

Today Intel is worth $272 billion.
TSMC is worth $1.6 trillion.

Would you have trusted the spreadsheet or Steve Jobs in 2006?

In 1951, doctors cut out King George VI's cancerous lung in a guest room at Buckingham Palace, and they never told him it was cancer.

When he died in his sleep a few months later at 56, the official cause was a blood clot in his heart.

Seventy-five years later, his great-grandson's wife made a whole film about her own cancer, and it's going out on BBC One and NBC.

Just look at what the palace did to keep 1951 quiet. Surgeons turned the Buhl Room, a first-floor guest room, into an operating theatre. Staff at Westminster Hospital noticed instruments and an entire operating table go missing, and nobody told them why. They even moved the Changing of the Guard to St James's Palace so the noise wouldn't reach the surgeons. The notice pinned to the palace gates blamed "structural changes" in the lung.

And here's the part that gets me. The Buhl Room is where Charles had been born three years earlier. On February 5, 2024, that baby, by then King, told the whole world he had cancer. That was one day short of 72 years after his grandfather died.

Seven weeks after that, Kate sat on a bench at Windsor and said the word herself. This June she climbed Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Snowdon inside 24 hours, which is 23 miles and more than 10,000 feet of climbing. The palace says no royal had done it before. Heal is the film of that climb, and every pound it makes goes to the Royal Marsden.

That hospital started with a cancer death too. A London surgeon named William Marsden lost his wife Betsy-Ann to cancer in 1846, and five years later he opened the first hospital in the world built only for cancer patients, back when he admitted medicine knew "absolutely nothing about it." Kate was treated there over what she called "many quiet, private visits."

A family that once kept the word cancer from its own King now has a future Queen saying it on prime-time TV in four countries.

A new open-source project called Leonida has appeared on GitHub to statically recompile the Xbox Series version of Grand Theft Auto VI into a native PC build. The tool translates console system calls and all 26,503 RDNA2 shaders into SPIR-V for the Vulkan API using files from the user's own game copy.

The game does not boot yet due to a missing executable and an incomplete D3D12 to Vulkan translation layer. However, the toolkit already successfully exports 3D models to OBJ, textures to DDS, and audio banks to Ogg Opus or WAV.

Building the port locally requires a copy of version 1.0.2.1, 350 GB of free disk space, Python 3.12, .NET 8 SDK, Vulkan SDK, LLVM 21, and Visual Studio 2022.

Here is my initial FSD v15 review after driving with it all afternoon and evening:

First off, Elon was right. This update is a BANGER! Tesla Reality View is out of this world and so insanely cool I’m still trying to process it all. 

FSD V15.0.1 brings so many improvements behind the scenes, in addition to the wildly cool UI. 

Tesla Reality View IS AMAZING! Pictures and video don’t do it any justice, this is something that has to be experienced to truly understand. Got to take a few friends tonight on drives to show them and every single person was blown away by it. The amount of detail it shows and generates is wild and so impressive. It shows reflection in the car, buildings, trees, turn arrows on the display and more. 

FSD v15 now has pothole avoidance! I had it swerve and avoid/straddle a few potholes tonight that were difficult for me to see in the dark.

Another great new feature in FSD v15 is speed camera slowdown. As you approach a speed camera, it automatically slows smoothly to the speed limit if you are in a quicker profile. This is a huge quality of life improvement especially as more cities get speed cameras. 

Parking seems near unchanged from the last build, I feel it picking spots quicker especially at the supercharger I went to tonight. Seems to be preferring to park in the first or second open spot it sees which is great, but it tried to park in one handicap spot- otherwise good. By far, the coolest part is Tesla Reality View. Holy crap is it insane to watch while parking. It’s the best backup/360 camera money can buy and such a detailed and clear view. 

Another new change I haven’t seen many people talk about is the turn signal fade. On FSD, the turn signal sound gets quieter after a few clicks. This is so nice if you’re sitting at a red light and makes drives more peaceful. 

Quiet Mode is also so nice at night. It darkens the display and just shows arrival time; music, climate on the bottom and a quick grok button on the top. Another feature that makes it feel like a Robotaxi UI and a peaceful supervising experience.

Another improvement is much better handling of dips and speed bumps. The past couple updates it’s been a bit too fast in my Model Y, and it’s now so smooth.

The nag is definitely reduced. The last couple versions of v14.3 had been sometimes a bit strict, but definitely more relaxed in v15.0.1. Another thing I noticed is way less wiper washing, a very welcome change. 

Personalized parking preferences are SO cool. At home, I can click on a person icon on the map and choose street parking or driveway, and it backs into the driveway EXACTLY in the spot I park my Model Y. It leared where I park and knows it. 

It also now lets you choose which lot you want to park in if the mall or store has multiple lots, you can select it on the map, worked at the mall, Costco, and Home Depot tonight. 

I need to touch on Tesla Reality View again because it’s just that cool. It really feels like you’re in a video game like NFS or GTA. I’m blown away by this and didn’t expect it at all. Tesla teams COOKED with it, I’ve seen so many on X now wanting Teslas because of it. I drove down Rodeo Drive tonight as well as by the SpaceX Falcon 9 and the views were so cool. Another place it’s cool is in wooded areas or tree filled streets, the way it shows everything is spectacular. Parking garages also give a cool look to them with the roof incorporated into the top of the UI. I didn’t think FSD could get this much better, as it was already so good and it did. 

I absolutely can’t wait to see what else is coming in the future and driving this more on road trips.

@elonmusk, you were right- V15 is incredible and super human! Huge congrats to the Tesla team on this, what a sick update. @TeslaSI and UI teams did a fantastic job, thank you all.

Out of everything posted about FSD v15 so far, one line from @elonmusk deserves way more attention than it's getting: "This is real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator. Let that sink in …" 🔥

Half of one accelerator is the part worth sitting with. Once you see the numbers behind it, Reality View stops looking like a fancy new screen and starts looking like one of the most impressive things Tesla has ever shipped.

🎬 THE SCREEN IS NOW GENERATED LIVE

For years, FSD's screen worked like a video game. Software took a list of what the car detected and dropped stock 3D models in the right spots: a gray car here, a lane line there.

Reality View tosses that playbook out the window. The car's AI now generates the video itself, frame after frame, as you drive, with no game engine anywhere in the loop.

Better yet, the picture comes from the same end-to-end model that's doing the driving. That's the single neural network that turns camera video into steering and braking, and now it paints your screen, too.

⚙️ WHAT A TRIP ACTUALLY IS

The standard AI4 computer carries two self-driving chips, and each chip packs three custom neural processors Tesla calls TRIP accelerators. That's six in all.

And that's where Reality View gets made: right on the self-driving computer, instead of the infotainment chip that runs your maps and music.

Each TRIP is basically an arena packed with tiny calculators, all cranking through the multiply-and-add math that neural networks run on. Teardowns count 9,216 of them per TRIP, lined up in a 96-by-96 grid and firing 2.2 billion times a second.

Each calculator handles two operations per tick, so one TRIP works out to 9,216 × 2 × 2.2 billion, or roughly 40 trillion operations every second.

Half of one comes to about 20 trillion, roughly a twelfth of the whole computer's neural muscle.

📏 WHY THAT NUMBER IS RIDICULOUS

Twenty trillion operations per second sounds enormous, until you see what else runs on that kind of budget.

The Neural Engine inside Apple's iPhone 15 Pro is rated at 35 trillion operations per second. So on paper, the slice of compute painting Reality View has less raw AI muscle than the AI chip in a 2023 phone.

Companies don't all count these numbers the same way, so it's a ballpark, but it shows just how little compute this is.

At the other end of the scale sits Nvidia's H100, one of the data-center workhorses powering today's AI boom. It's rated at about 1,979 trillion 8-bit operations per second in its standard mode, the same kind of math a TRIP runs, which puts half a TRIP at roughly 1% of one H100.

That gap matters because AI video is one of the toughest jobs in AI. Many AI video generators still take minutes to produce a single clip, as the researchers behind the real-time system MotionStream point out.

Even MotionStream, built specifically for speed, streams roughly 17 to 29 frames per second at 480p, and about 10 at 720p, while eating up an entire H100.

Meanwhile, Tesla is streaming a live, photorealistic view of the real road on roughly 1% of that chip's rated power, inside a moving car.

In other words, Reality View runs on less compute than a phone's AI chip, inside a computer whose main job is driving.

There's a fair asterisk here. Those research models dream up whole scenes from a prompt or a single image, while Tesla's renderer starts with a driving brain that already knows exactly what's around the car. Tesla also hasn't shared the view's resolution or frame rate.

And even on the most generous estimates of AI4's power, half a TRIP still works out to only about 2% of one H100.

Either way, live generated video on a sliver of a car computer would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

🔍 HOW IT CAN BE THIS CHEAP

Tesla hasn't spelled out how it works, but it has left plenty of breadcrumbs.

FSD's network has been building its own 3D picture of the world for a while now, something Tesla showed off at the ICCV conference in October 2025. That picture includes 3D Gaussians, millions of soft little blobs of color that can rebuild a scene you can view from any angle.

Tesla also built its own Gaussian splatting system that can rebuild a scene from the car's cameras in a fraction of a second.

Reality View streams its picture from a virtual camera that can sit anywhere above the car, and showing a scene from an angle no real camera has is exactly what those 3D blobs are great at.

Even Elon seems to like that theory: he called a description of Reality View as a neural, Gaussian-splat digital twin "pretty accurate", and it lines up with every other clue.

If that's the trick, the hard part is done before the screen ever needs a picture. The driving brain understands the scene, and the visualization just paints what it already knows.

That would explain the other shocker. Reality View swapped every separate signal behind the old screen for one end-to-end visualization, and it still uses less compute than the bare-bones 2020 visualization did.

🚗 WHY TESLA CARES SO MUCH

v15 is Tesla's large model, built to squeeze every ounce of performance out of HW4. On a chip working that hard, a screen that costs half of one TRIP leaves nearly everything else for the driving.

And it's a flex, too. The AI4 computer costs about $650 by Elon's own figure, and that same box now drives the car and paints live video of the world at the same time.

This is only the start. Elon says Tesla vehicles will share traffic knowledge and combine it with Grok's real-time 𝕏 feed, even giving you a heads-up about what's happening at your destination.

A view this cheap to generate is the perfect canvas for that kind of shared knowledge.

Elon asked everyone to let that sink in, and the math earns it: half of one accelerator in a $650 computer is painting the real world live while FSD drives.
